summary: Background. Frailty is often raised as a reason to withhold complete revascularization from older patients after myocardial infarction, although the FIRE trial found no interaction between frailty and the benefit of physiology-guided complete revascularization. Objective. To estimate the cost-effectiveness of physiology-guided complete versus culprit-lesion-only revascularization after successful culprit-lesion percutaneous coronary intervention in patients aged 75 years or older with myocardial infarction and multivessel disease, overall and across Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) strata, from the German statutory health insurance perspective. Methods. A three-year cohort model with quarterly cycles was anchored to the FIRE marginal outcomes (primary composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or ischaemia-driven revascularization 22.9% versus 29.8%; cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction 12.8% versus 18.2%; heart-failure hospitalisation 14.3% versus 19.7%). Risks in CFS 1-3, 4 and 5-9 were obtained by external calibration that preserved these trial marginals, with a relative treatment effect common to all strata. Costs used 2026 German diagnosis-related-group tariffs. Every input was classified by provenance, and uncertainty was assessed with 20,000 probabilistic draws, one-way and scenario analyses, and break-even analysis. Results. Complete revascularization cost EUR 757 more per patient and yielded 0.056 additional quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of EUR 13,601 per QALY. Ratios were EUR 20,541 per QALY in CFS 1-3, EUR 8,640 in CFS 4 and EUR 8,662 in CFS 5-9. The probability of cost-effectiveness at EUR 30,000 per QALY was 92.5% overall and 78.6%, 96.5% and 97.7% across strata. At that value, the minimum three-year absolute reduction in the primary composite required for cost-effectiveness was 4.3 per 100 patients overall, against a modelled trial effect of 6.9. Staging the additional procedure as a separate admission was the most influential cost driver. Conclusions. Within three years, physiology-guided complete revascularization appears cost-effective at reference values of EUR 20,000 to EUR 50,000 per QALY, and estimated cost-effectiveness was not attenuated in the frailer strata. The stratum-specific estimates rest on external frailty calibration rather than on frailty-specific FIRE outcomes and are not evidence of effect modification.
title: Cost-Effectiveness of Physiology-Guided Complete Revascularization Across Frailty Strata in Older Patients with Myocardial Infarction: A German Analysis Informed by the FIRE Trial

summary: Revision of the dataset prepared during peer review of the accompanying data descriptor at IEEE Data Descriptions . The 94 satellite–in-situ pairs and their concentration values are unchanged; what changes is how records are identified in time, what per-reservoir metadata is provided, and what guidance ships with the raw processor columns. Breaking change samples.csv no longer has a Date column. It is replaced by Campaign , with the values Summer YYYY and Autumn YYYY . The monitoring network samples these reservoirs twice a year, in June and in November, and the campaign label is what the compiled matchup table retains; the literal dates in v1.0.0 were a downstream conversion and should not be read as acquisition timestamps. Code written against v1.0.0 must be updated. Per-record acquisition timestamps were not retained when the table was compiled, so the individual in-situ/satellite temporal offsets cannot be recovered from these files. What is documented is the characterisation reported with the original processing (Cuartero et al., 2023): all 94 images fall inside the ±48 h selection window and 26% were acquired on the same day as the in-situ sample. Records cannot be filtered by temporal offset; studies for which simultaneity is critical should treat the whole collection as subject to an offset of up to two days. Added metadata.csv gains two morphometric descriptors per reservoir (15 → 17 columns): Eq. width (pix) , the equivalent width √A in 10 m pixels, and Window fraction (%) , the share of the water surface covered by a single 7×7 extraction window. Across the network the window fraction ranges from 0.26% to 49%. Users are advised to discard or treat separately any reservoir above about 25%. baseline_correction.py , a self-contained script (NumPy and pandas only) that fits a log–log correction log10(Chl) = a·log10(P) + b for each processor, plus a joint form over the three co-registered retrievals, and evaluates it under leave-one-reservoir-out cross-validation. Out-of-sample, it brings C2X from 639% to 39% MAPD and C2XC from 2181% to 43%; the joint form reaches 18%. It is a starting point and a sanity check, not a recommended retrieval, and its coefficients should not be transferred to other networks without refitting. Changed README updated for the new columns and the script, with a provenance note on time and a note on modelling with unevenly sampled reservoirs (Gini 0.32; effective number of equally weighted reservoirs 21.9 of 32). Use the reservoir, not the record, as the unit of resampling. The dataset is now named C2NEx-22, and the accompanying descriptor is identified as submitted to IEEE Data Descriptions .
title: C2NEx-22: A Paired Satellite–in-situ Chlorophyll-a in Extremadura, Spain for 32 Reservoirs Dataset

summary: This record contains the complete R and Python code and supporting documentation for the independent sensitivity reanalysis associated with the manuscript “Swab-based stool collection largely preserves gut microbiome structure with small device-dependent effects: an intra-individual evaluation of sampling devices and processing conditions.” The archive includes scripts to reconstruct and validate anonymous sample metadata from the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) run report and FASTQ filenames; perform preliminary read-quality and paired-read overlap assessments; process forward (R1) and reverse (R2) reads separately using DADA2; infer ASVs; assign taxonomy using the SILVA SSU NR99 release 138.2 training set; construct phylogenetic trees; evaluate sequencing-depth dependence; calculate standardized alpha- and beta-diversity metrics, including Faith’s phylogenetic diversity, weighted UniFrac, and Bray–Curtis dissimilarity; compare the R1 and R2 results; assess sensitivity to rarefaction depth and unusually long terminal branches; and generate the corresponding tables and figures. The archive also contains a complete execution guide, software dependencies and versions, random seeds, original R session information, reference-database details, and file-integrity checksums. Sample metadata and analytical outputs are generated locally by the documented workflow and are not distributed as precomputed files. Raw paired-end sequencing data are publicly available from the European Nucleotide Archive under accession PRJEB107991. The DADA2-formatted SILVA 138.2 taxonomic training set is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14169026 . The independent ASV analyses complement, but do not reproduce or replace, the proprietary MicrobAT® workflow used for the primary OTU-based analysis. MicrobAT® algorithms, OTU-assignment parameters, and the release of its embedded reference database were not disclosed by the software provider. Accordingly, this archive supports reproducibility of the independent R1/R2 ASV sensitivity analyses and downstream analyses of the published MicrobAT® outputs, but not reconstruction of the proprietary MicrobAT®-generated OTU and taxonomic profiles. summary: Our earlier note (rejected from an SC26 AI4S workshop, subsequently published as AIIT Bulletin Vol. 20) compared classical reduced-order models (POD, DMD) against naive neural surrogates (a fully-connected network, a CNN) on textbook-scale problems (lid-driven cavity, dam-break), on a single consumer GPU workstation. That note left five concrete gaps: no graph-based neural baseline, no industrially complex geometry, weak statistical evidence (nine snapshots, a single seed), no learned-dynamics counterpart to DMD, and no hyperparameter search for the neural baselines. This paper closes four of those five. The test case is an industrially representative two-phase stirred tank — a six-blade rotating impeller on a sliding (AMI) mesh, a bottom sparger injecting gas into water, ∼167k cells, solved with OpenFOAM's twoPhaseEulerFoam — run entirely on a single Mac Studio (Apple M4 Max, 14 cores, no discrete GPU). We benchmark five methods (POD, DMD, a neural network, a Graph Neural Operator, and a Deep Koopman autoencoder) on a genuine extrapolation task, backed by a 400-run statistical-robustness sweep, hyperparameter searches for both neural baselines, a check across three impeller speeds, and a four-level forcing-irregularity sweep (quasi-periodic through chaotic, direction-reversing impeller motion) intended to locate DMD's failure point. DMD wins consistently across every data scale, truncation choice, operating condition, and forcing-irregularity level tested, at both a 1 s and an extended 3 s prediction horizon – we did not find the failure threshold we went looking for, and report that directly. The search was not wasted, however: a Deep Koopman autoencoder, competitive at 1 s, degrades sharply at 3 s from compounding autoregressive rollout error (exposure bias); two independent, cheap mitigations – a physical [0, 1] clip mirroring the Graph Neural Operator's own implicit stabilization, and multi-step scheduled-sampling training – each recover roughly a third to a half of the gap without closing it, confirming the diagnosis. A separate, unplanned check turns up a sharper result: ranking methods by mass conservation rather than per-cell accuracy reorders them completely, with the most accurate method (DMD) only third-best at holding a basic physical invariant. We treat all three investigations as concrete instances of a broader, practical question for this community: how much genuine, open-ended scientific investigation — not just a fixed benchmark — can a single high-end workstation support before an HPC allocation is actually necessary? All code, case files, and Colab notebooks are released on GitHub for reproduction.
title: How Far Does One Workstation Go? A Pre-HPC Efficiency Check for Industrial-Scale CFD and Reduced-Order Model Benchmarking

summary: FPGA-Accelerated Sub-Microsecond Union-Find Decoding for Real-Time Surface-Code Quantum Memory Architecture manuscript. Latency, power, and resource figures are design estimates unless otherwise marked as measured. Related FPGA Union-Find implementations (Helios / Collision Clustering) are cited for comparison. Abstract Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires continuous decoding of stabilizer syndromes within cycle times that, for superconducting processors, are often 200 ns–1 μs. Host-processor decoders are subject to operating-system jitter, DMA overhead, and memory-hierarchy latency, which make deterministic sub-microsecond service difficult. This paper describes a fully pipelined FPGA architecture for a Union-Find decoder aimed at surface-code quantum memory. The pipeline integrates Aurora-based syndrome acquisition, streaming defect extraction, a path-halving Union-Find engine with hazard forwarding, localized peeling, and dual-port Pauli-frame updates. All latency-critical state is on-chip (BRAM, UltraRAM, distributed RAM). At a target clock of 400 MHz the design estimate for end-to-end latency is 170–390 ns below threshold, with a conservative worst-case bound near 500 ns—inside a 1 μs cycle. Memory for a decoding window scales as O(d³) with the space-time graph, not as O(d³) measurements per cycle. Power is estimated at 3–6 W per logical patch at the FPGA, which remains at room temperature. The contribution is a single deterministic pipeline that does not require a host CPU in the inner loop. It is an architecture and resource plan; it does not replace measured implementations such as Helios. Keywords: surface code; quantum error correction; Union-Find decoder; FPGA; real-time decoding; Pauli frame; clock gating. 1. Introduction Surface-code fault tolerance proceeds by repeated stabilizer measurement and classical decoding of the syndrome stream [1], [9], [10]. Superconducting cycle times commonly fall in T_cycle ~ 200 ns–1 μs [13]. Software decoders on CPUs or GPUs introduce scheduling jitter, DMA cost, cache misses, and synchronization [14]–[16]. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) is accurate but worst-case cubic in the number of defects and heavy for large distance [17], [18]. The Union-Find decoder of Delfosse and Nickerson is almost-linear and close to MWPM in accuracy, which makes it a natural hardware target [3]. FPGA and ASIC decoders have already shown that real-time surface-code decoding is possible. Das et al. gave a Union-Find micro-architecture; Liyanage et al. (Helios) implemented distributed Union-Find on a VCU129 up to d = 21 with mean times of order 10 ns per round under phenomenological noise, and a resource-optimized d = 51 point near 544 ns per round [14], [15]. Collision Clustering, another Union-Find variant, has been mapped to FPGA and ASIC with sub-microsecond times at large patch size [16]. The present manuscript specifies a single-tile, fully streaming pipeline—acquisition through Pauli frame—with explicit memory equations, banked Find ports, path-halving (not recursive compression), clock-enable power control, and a latency budget written against T_cycle = 1 μs. It is intended as a self-contained hardware architecture that can be implemented or compared against those measured designs. 2. System Architecture The decoder is a fixed-depth pipeline. Stages are registered and advance on the same clock. After fill, a new syndrome frame can be accepted every cycle from the control layer; variable work inside Union-Find is bounded by a worst-case iteration budget, not by a host thread. Stages: •     Syndrome acquisition and deserialization (Aurora 64B/66B over GTY). •     Defect extraction unit (DEU): frame-to-frame XOR and sparse packing. •     Pipelined Union-Find engine: growth, union, path-halving find, boundary test. •     Localized peeling
title: FPGA-Accelerated Sub-Microsecond Union-Find Decoding for Real-Time Surface-Code Quantum Memory

files.key: Two Experimental Protocols for Verifying the Dominance of Internal Information in RNA From the Error Threshold to Protocell Construction.pdf

summary: The RNA world hypothesis faces two core challenges: first, the error threshold paradox—the contradiction between the length required for RNA replication and its fidelity; second, the transition from free RNA to a primitive cell (membrane-encapsulated system)—how to spontaneously form a selectively permeable compartmental structure. Dual Information Cybernetics states that internal information (the intrinsic determinacy of a system) possesses four attributes: wholeness, potentiality, self-consistency, and dominance. Among these, dominance drives the system from disorder to order and delimits the boundary of possibility for all local processes. Based on this theory, this paper proposes two mutually supporting experimental protocols: (1) the RNA condensate experiment—under mild wet-dry cycling conditions, observing whether RNA with secondary structure spontaneously forms condensates and testing whether the replication fidelity within the condensate is higher than that of single molecules, thereby verifying that "collective synergy" can bypass the error threshold; (2) the RNA-lipid co-assembly experiment—under the same mild conditions, observing whether RNA actively attracts lipid molecules and drives vesicle formation, forming an RNA-containing protocell model, thereby verifying the "active nest-building" behavior driven by the dominance of internal information. Both experiments share the same theoretical framework and mild-condition design; their results corroborate each other and can provide direct visualizable evidence for the dominance of internal information. This paper describes in detail the experimental materials, apparatus, observational indicators, expected results, and significance, aiming to provide an actionable research protocol for experimental researchers and to advance the information-theoretic perspective on the origin of life.
title: Two Experimental Protocols for Verifying the Dominance of Internal Information in RNA From the Error Threshold to Protocell Construction

summary: Full Changelog : https://github.com/attogram/fantastic-octo-giggle/compare/0001...0002 42 and the Open Error Foundation: An Academic Interpretation Abstract The relationship between 42 and the Open Error Foundation (i.o.) can be understood as more than a recurring joke, reference, or organizational number. It can function as a compact epistemological model for the Foundation itself. The central problem of 42 is not that the answer is numerically wrong. It is that an answer can be generated before the question has been adequately established. That distinction is extraordinarily relevant to an organization concerned with artificial intelligence, institutional systems, scientific error, education, and continuous experimentation. The Foundation's two central statements, "Error is the message" and "Sesame Street is the teacher," consequently form a complementary methodology. The first treats failure, contradiction, mismatch, and unexpected output as potentially informative evidence. The second establishes a method for responding to uncertainty: return to fundamentals, ask understandable questions, experiment, explain, repeat, and learn. 42 then represents the unresolved question at the center of the entire process. The organization does not claim to possess the ultimate answer. It asks whether we have actually identified the question. The 42 Problem: An Answer Without a Question The cultural origin of 42 is Douglas Adams' The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. Within the story, the enormous computer Deep Thought spends millions of years calculating the answer to the "Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything." The result is: The fundamental joke is subsequently revealed: the beings who commissioned the computation do not actually know what the Ultimate Question is. A later computational project is therefore required to determine the question itself. This creates a particularly interesting epistemological structure: Question → computation → answer has been replaced by: computation → answer → realization that the question is unknown → search for the question That reversal is precisely what makes 42 relevant to AI. A modern AI system can produce an extraordinarily fluent answer to an inadequately specified question. It can produce something that looks like knowledge before the underlying problem has been properly framed. The resulting failure is therefore not necessarily: "The machine calculated incorrectly." It may instead be: "We never established what needed to be calculated." That is a much deeper category of error. Error Is the Message The Open Error Foundation's phrase "Error is the message" can therefore be interpreted as an epistemological proposition rather than simply a creative slogan. Ordinarily, error is treated as something to eliminate: correct → incorrect → remove incorrect But scholarship in the philosophy and history of science has explicitly examined the possibility that errors can have productive epistemic roles. Jutta Schickore's historical analysis argues that error can contribute to scientific practice rather than merely obstruct it. More recently, Douglas Allchin's Toward a Philosophy of Error in Science develops an explicit framework around "error analytics," including error types, error signatures, checkpoints, error probes, and negative knowledge. His argument is that scientific practice is not merely about accumulating confirmations; it also depends on systematically identifying and managing ways in which knowledge can fail. This provides a serious academic foundation for the Foundation's intuition. An error can contain information about: the assumptions behind a system the limits of a model the framing of a question the quality of available evidence hidden dependencies institutional incentives human misunderstanding the difference between intended and actual behavior In this interpretation: An error is an observation about a system. The Open Error Foundation can therefore be understood as prac

files.key: HKD_FACTOR_50 Secure Data Valuation and Sharing via Homomorphic Encryption.pdf

summary: Abstract Data marketplaces and collaborative analytics require a way to estimate the value of contributed records without exposing the records themselves. This paper presents HKD_FACTOR_50, a protocol architecture that com-bines task-specific marginal-contribution valuation, addi-tively homomorphic aggregation, policy-bound release, and an auditable payment ledger. The construction does not claim that encryption makes arbitrary machine-learning training private. Instead, it protects a deliber-ately restricted interface: contributors encrypt quantized valuation statistics, an evaluator computes approved linear aggregates on ciphertexts, and a threshold or designated decryptor releases only authorized totals. We define cor-rectness, confidentiality, integrity, and audit requirements; describe leakage and collusion boundaries; and provide a complete executable Python reference demonstration based on the Paillier cryptosystem. The program verifies encrypted weighted aggregation against plaintext compu-tation and rejects tampered ledger entries. The reference code is pedagogical rather than production-hardened, but it makes the protocol’s data flow and invariants repro-ducible. HKD_FACTOR_50 therefore supplies a concrete baseline for privacy-preserving data valuation while iden-tifying the additional controls required for deployment: authenticated transport, robust key custody, range proofs, differential-privacy release, and independently reviewed cryptographic libraries. Keywords Data valuation; homomorphic encryption; authenticate participants, and control what is released. privacy-preserving computation; Paillier cryptosystem; secure data sharing; auditability; data marketplace; Shapley value.
title: HKD_FACTOR_50: Secure Data Valuation and Sharing via Homomorphic Encryption

summary: A three-signal stopping rule for iterative LLM refinement derived from the Möbius theory stack: an equilibrium-distance surrogate d̂_R (RZGM meaning-equilibrium layer), an update-free-recurrence and diversity-collapse detector pair (Reflective Homeostasis Layer), and a hard reflection-depth cap (MUSE bounded reflection). Pre-registered study: 500 English prose-refinement tasks across ten domains, two generator models (Gemma4 12B-IT-QAT and 26B-A4B-IT-QAT), 8,000 generations, 999 blind position-swapped pairwise judgments. The governor cuts refinement tokens by 36.6% / 33.1% (bootstrap 95% CIs 33.6-39.5% / 30.3-35.9%) versus an always-eight-iterations baseline — 2.2-3.4x a naive convergence stop — at a measured quality cost reported at equal prominence: 38.0% / 36.6% of judged comparisons lost overall, a majority among actual interventions (61.1% / 59.0%), with measured cost almost perfectly collinear with output length. A full-data ablation shows the saturation signal is simultaneously the savings engine and the dominant cost source, yielding a measured two-point dial (10.0-11.5% savings at 8.2-11.8% loss rate with saturation disabled). Pre-release adversarial verification (four independent refuter passes) confirmed all headline statistics against the raw data and caught an inverted flagship anecdote: the corpus's two catastrophic degenerations (~50 verbatim paragraph repetitions) were selected once and avoided once by the governor, undetected in both cases — set-based trigram signals are structurally blind to within-output verbatim repetition. All tasks, rollouts, verdicts, audit votes, and analysis code are released in the companion repository. AI co-observer: Claude Fable 5 (Anthropic) — working method only; blind pairwise judging by Claude subagents under a position-swapped two-vote protocol; four independent adversarial refuter passes preceded release; the registered author is the human author alone. Version 1.1 (2026-09-19): adds (i) a proof-backed clarification that at window 3 the saturation condition is exactly “three identical consecutive non-rewrite change types” (the 0.70 threshold is inert there; companion note DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22842506), (ii) a pre-registered evaluation of a repetition-ratio guard as a fourth, roll-back signal — fires on both known collapses and 200/200 synthetic inflations, on 0 of 7,998 remaining published generations, 0 of 60 template expansions, and 0 of 960 held-out generations (verdict GO; pre-registration commit a89f722 precedes all evaluation data), and (iii) an expanded AI-authorship disclosure. All v1.0 numbers are unchanged. Version 1.2 (2026-09-19): adds (i) a length-stratified reanalysis of the 621 judged governor pairs (loss rate 92% where the early text is under 60% of the final length, 16.1% at near-equal length; 31 losses vs 4 wins at matched length, sign test p < 10 -5 — evidence of a content cost independent of length, not a decomposition of the headline cost), (ii) a held-out replication on 60 tasks authored after the fourth-signal pre-registration (token reduction 34.5% / 34.5%, loss rate 31.7% / 36.7%, main-study values inside the held-out intervals), and (iii) an online-intervention verification: an incremental governor reproduces all 1,000 published decisions (0 mismatches) and, run as a genuine online loop on the 60 held-out tasks with the 12B generator, generates 319 of 480 iterations with a stop distribution indistinguishable from the offline policy (permutation p = 0.46). All v1.0 and v1.1 numbers are unchanged. Version 1.3 (2026-09-19): adds a pre-registered length-matched re-judging (100 governor-loss pairs with early/final length ratio < 0.80; final text truncated at sentence boundaries to the early text's word count): the early text beats the length-matched final in 94/100 (loss 4%), and the full final beats its own truncation in 100/100. Pre-registered label: the losses on this stratum are attributab
title: The Reflective Budget Governor: Equilibrium-Based Early Stopping for Iterative LLM Refinement

summary: This repository contains the official R implementation and replication scripts for the research paper: "Evaluating Feature Selection for Uncertainty Quantification in Digital Soil Mapping: A Case Study of Soil pH" . Overview Digital Soil Mapping (DSM) frameworks require robust feature selection (FS) to mitigate collinearity and enhance spatial prediction while properly characterizing predictive uncertainties. This study systematically evaluates six feature selection methods across five machine learning and quantile regression models for soil pH mapping. Workflow Components Feature Selection Methods (6): Variance Inflation Factor ( VIF ) Recursive Feature Elimination ( RFE ) Simulated Annealing variants ( SA-FS1 , SA-FS2 ) Genetic Algorithm variants ( GA-FS1 , GA-FS2 ) Machine Learning Algorithms (5): Support Vector Machine ( SVM ) Random Forest ( RF ) Cubist ( Cubist ) Extreme Gradient Boosting ( XGBoost ) Quantile Random Forest ( QRF ) Evaluation & Uncertainty Quantification (UQ): Scripts include parameter tuning, cross-validation workflows, point estimation metrics (RMSE, MAE, R²), and uncertainty quantification diagnostics (prediction interval coverage probability, interval width, and spatial uncertainty mapping). Repository Structure The scripts are structured into dedicated subfolders for each of the five models, providing standalone execution pipelines for feature selection, model fitting, and uncertainty estimation. Data Availability Due to institutional data-sharing policies and privacy considerations, the raw spatial and soil sample datasets are not hosted in this repository. Users can adapt the provided pipelines to their own raster covariates and soil point observation tables. Data access inquiries can be directed to the corresponding author upon reasonable request. Citation If you find this code useful in your research, please cite the corresponding publication (details provided in the README and publication metadata).
title: Feature Selection Framework for Uncertainty Quantification in Digital Soil Mapping

summary: We propose a synthetic-trained adaptive radial prediction filter for reversible quaternion graph lifting. Controlled synthetic regimes vary seven geometry factors; regime-optimal admissible filters are compressed into three prototypes. A seven-component decoder-visible descriptor drives a lightweight mixture estimator, with both bank and estimator trained entirely on synthetic data and frozen for target deployment. A parameter-free reference-routed update preserves exact reconstruction. On TotalCapture, the method reduces geodesic prediction MSE by   versus a nonadaptive cubic B-spline predictor that uses a single   radial filter across all neighborhoods, and   versus uniform Karcher averaging, without target-domain fitting or transmitted node-wise adaptation parameters.
title: Synthetic-Trained Radial Adaptation for Quaternion Graph Lifting

summary: Raw and processed data, instrument configuration and analysis code from an experimental campaign on evaporation suppression by a modular floating cover, carried out between 14 August and 11 September 2026 at the Department of Nuclear Energy, Federal University of Pernambuco, Recife, Brazil (8.0476 S, 34.8769 W, 10 m a.s.l.). A Class A evaporation pan of 1.185 m internal diameter (1.1029 m2 free surface) was instrumented with a Campbell Scientific CR1000 datalogger recording at a 1 min interval: water level (QDY30A hydrostatic transducer), incident short-wave irradiance (Kipp & Zonen SP-LITE, with a LI-COR LI200X as secondary sensor), air temperature and relative humidity (Vaisala HMP45C), water temperature at three depths (Campbell 108 thermistors) and air velocity (Campbell 034A/034B). Radiative forcing was supplied by a dimmer-controlled array of 18 infrared drying lamps of 250 W, and advection by a fan discharging horizontally across the water surface. The floating cover consisted of rigid hexagonal plates of 110 mm side, deployed as 27 plates (77.0 % coverage) or 26 plates (74.1 % coverage), in two geometries. Fifteen experimental windows span three advective regimes (about 2 m/s, about 3.3 m/s and no forced air flow) and irradiance from 106 to 940 W/m2. On 10 September the sensors were repositioned and pH and conductivity probes added; records from that date describe a different instrument geometry and are excluded from every window. Twenty photographs of the apparatus are included, each described in a caption file. The deposit contains the unmodified TOA5 record, a consolidated 1 min series with vapour pressure deficit and latent heat flux added, a table of evaporation rates for each experimental window obtained by linear regression of water level against time, the Python script that reproduces both processed files from the raw record, the CRBasic measurement program and the sensor wiring documentation. The README describes every column, its unit, the -99.999 missing-data sentinel and the time bounds of each window, including the exclusion of the buoyancy transient that follows cover deployment. A separate folder holds five short commissioning exports from 12 and 13 August 2026, included as provenance for the acquisition system. They show that the hydrostatic level transducer entered the logger program at version v7 and that the air temperature and humidity probe began returning valid readings on 13 August. No result depends on them. Suppression is reported both as a raw ratio of rates and after normalising each rate by the mean vapour pressure deficit of its own window, because the two figures differ by up to 13.7 percentage points: covered and uncovered windows were run at different times of day and therefore under different atmospheric demand. The processing script reproduces both. These data support the manuscript "Vapour pressure deficit control reveals a stable suppression efficiency of modular hexagonal floating covers across advective regimes: a rate-based pan study for semiarid Brazil".
title: Evaporation suppression by modular hexagonal floating covers over an instrumented Class A pan (MAISSER-PE, Recife, Brazil, August 2026)

summary: Medicine-level dataset and complete R analysis code for the retrospective cohort study Authorised in Europe, Awaited in Bulgaria: A Time-to-Event Analysis of Where the 3.9-Year Delay to Oncology Medicine Reimbursement Accrues (Department of Social Medicine and Public Health, Medical University of Plovdiv, Bulgaria). summary: State observation over the Hamilton division algebra is formulated as a structured realization problem for quaternionic multi-input multi-output systems. A left-intertwiner equation unifies companion assignment, row-oriented robust pole assignment, and coupled target realization with explicit noncommutative product order. A unitary measured-subspace decomposition yields a derivative-free observer with n-r dynamic quaternion states, where r = rank C, and reduces observability and detectability to a smaller pair. This order is minimal within the stated quaternion-linear full-state observer class. For full-order observers, structured H2 Lyapunov equations and an exact fixed-target gradient allow noise attenuation without moving the spectrum. For minimum-order observers, the reconstruction exposes the direct noise term and its interaction with pole-invariant injection freedom. Discrete-time formulas include the finite contribution of direct feedthrough, and correlated redundant outputs are characterized as noise references. Reproducible studies verify the gradients, compare quaternion, structured-complex, and real representations, expose the noise-cost nonuniqueness of maximum-volume designs, and test coupled repeated-class targets and a multi-output minimum-order observer.
title: Full- and Minimum-Order Quaternionic MIMO Observers: Spectral Assignment and Noise Geometry

summary: This repository contains the data, documentation, and replication materials associated with the data paper on the  Cartulario de Santo Toribio de Liébana . The dataset provides a structured reconstruction of the documentary collection edited by Luis Sánchez Belda and converts the information contained in the cartulary into machine-readable research data. It covers 566 documentary acts and includes linked information on 576 payment or counter-performance elements, 603 place names, and 1,348 identified persons , together with a concordance between documentary numbering systems. The package preserves the documentary structure of the source while providing standardized variables suitable for quantitative and computational historical research. Particular attention is given to economic transactions. Payments and other forms of material counter-performance are recorded at the individual-component level rather than collapsed into a single transaction value. The data also distinguish operative contractual provisions from penalty clauses and other formulaic diplomatic material. Contains the materials required to reproduce and audit the construction of the dataset, including the structured datasets, extraction and coding documentation, variable definitions, provenance information, validation materials, and the code used for data processing and quality-control procedures. The replication workflow documents the transformation from the published documentary source to the final structured tables. It records corrections and normalization decisions while maintaining traceability to the underlying documentary act. The package is therefore intended not only to reproduce the published dataset but also to make individual coding decisions auditable. summary: Background: Dried Haritaki ( Terminalia chebula Retz.) fruit, Dried Amalaki ( Phyllanthus emblica L.) fruit, Dried Vidanga ( Embelia ribes Burm.f.) fruit, Dried Trivruta ( Operculina turpethum (L.) Silva Manso) root and Dried Haridra ( Curcuma longa L.) rhizome; These drugs require reliable diagnostic characteristics for authentication and quality control for use in treatment of Dadru (dermatophytosis) . This study comparatively evaluated their organoleptic, macroscopic, and powder-microscopic characteristics to identify key diagnostic features. Materials and Methods: Authenticated samples of Haritaki, Amalaki, Vidanga, Trivruta and Haridra were evaluated for their organoleptic, macroscopic and powder microscopic characteristics using standard pharmacognostical methods. Diagnostic features were documented by light microscopy and compared with pharmacopoeial references . Results: Pharmacognostical evaluation of Haritaki , Amalaki , Vidanga , Trivruta and Haridra confirmed their authenticity through organoleptic, macroscopic and powder microscopic examinations. Each drug exhibited distinct diagnostic features such as characteristic taste, odour, fracture, and microscopic markers including fibres, stone cells, starch grains, sclereids, vessels and oleoresin cells, consistent with pharmacopeial standards. Conclusion: The study established reproducible diagnostic parameters for the selected drugs, ensuring accurate identification and quality control. These findings provide baseline pharmacognostical data for quality assessment of the selected drugs intended for formulations used in Dadru (dermatophytosis).

summary: R code, input parameters and generated outputs reproducing every result of the accompanying article. The analysis is a decision-analytic state-transition (Markov) model comparing four strategies for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aficamten, mavacamten, alcohol septal ablation and septal myectomy, in Germany and the United States, with standard medical therapy as a secondary reference arm. It covers the four-strategy efficiency frontier, four separately defined annual acquisition-price thresholds, probabilistic sensitivity analysis over 10 000 draws with common random numbers, and an age-specific specification for starting ages 40 to 85 years using national life tables and published age-stratified procedural risks. Contents: 16 R scripts, two life-table input files, and 70 generated outputs (tables, figures and logs). Running "Rscript run_all.R" from a clean directory regenerates all of them. The run begins with an audit gate of 252 automated checks covering arithmetic identities, the provenance of every price, the separation of the four price concepts, the wording of categorical results, and the internal consistency of the cross-trial declaration. No output is written unless every check passes. No individual patient data are included or required. All inputs are published trial results, national tariff catalogues, national life tables and explicitly declared assumptions; each is listed with its source, or with the explicit absence of one, in the provenance register. Requires R 4.6.0 or later with ggplot2, dplyr, scales, patchwork, ggrepel and jsonlite.

summary: This manuscript identifies six substrates — individual memory, species lineages, externalised records, immune memory, the first generation of stars, and prion populations — which share a four-part mechanical structure, and among which no pair, to our knowledge, cites another. We specify the four mechanisms as an explicit screen, and validate it by applying it to cases that should fail: thermal equilibrium scores zero of four, sheared amorphous matter scores an intermediate two and a half, and stem cells score three of four in a manner that identifies precisely which mechanism is missing. We then derive, from this framework’s own commitment that any render of a record is necessarily partial, a scaling law governing all six: the more degraded the record, the more the reconstruction is determined by the template rather than by the record. We show this law is independently confirmed in four of the six fields, under four different names, by researchers not addressing one another. We supply a birth term that a companion manuscript’s earlier treatment lacked, deriving it from Bennett’s history-tape result rather than from biology, and show that a standard macroevolutionary survivorship formula then applies to memory unchanged. Three results that did not hold are recorded in full, including one prediction that failed outright on simulation and one correspondence that was stated backwards relative to the data. The foundational architecture, geometric intuitions, and motivating philosophy of this framework originated independently with the author prior to and separate from any AI involvement. Subsequent mathematical derivation, connection to established physics literature, computational verification, and error-checking were conducted through extended technical work with AI systems (Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Gemini). The author directed this process, evaluated and selected among proposed derivations, and takes full responsibility for the accuracy and originality of the final work.
title: Reconstruction from a Degraded Record: Six Substrates, One Scaling Law, and a Dispute Six Fields Have Independently

summary: Metrics Added MixtureMetric and MixtureComponent , which express a weighted linear combination of BaseMetric instances. This is exact, by linearity of expectation, and is how empcs_score now expresses a distribution that mixes a point mass with a continuous piece — something a single Metric cannot express, since SymPy cannot symbolically integrate over such a distribution. Added BaseMetric , the abstraction every loss parameter throughout the package now accepts. Metric and MixtureMetric both implement it, so either can be passed interchangeably as a model's training objective. Added the LogCost strategy for building custom expected log cost (weighted cross-entropy) metrics. expected_log_cost_loss is now built from it. Metrics built with the Cost and Savings strategies now accept stochastic ( sympy.stats ) cost parameters, reducing them to their mean. Previously this raised NotImplementedError: Random variables are not supported for the savings metric. at Metric construction time. Added constrain and constrain , which declare the values a cost-matrix parameter is allowed to take. A parameter can be given inclusive lower / upper bounds, or a callable can express a condition spanning several parameters at once ( constrain(lambda p: p['clv'] > p['incentive_cost'], message=...) ). Added Profit , MinCost and EmpiricalMinCost , the sign-flipped siblings of Cost , MaxProfit and EmpiricalMaxProfit . Each computes the same quantity as its partner and reports it with the opposite sign, so a cost matrix can be read as costs to minimize or as profits to maximize. The choice is presentational: the optimal threshold and rate are unchanged, and models fit identically on either member of a pair. Added EmpiricalMaxProfit and AUEPC strategies for building custom metrics that compute the empirical (convex-hull-based) maximum profit and the area under the empirical profit curve, respectively. Metric now warns ( UserWarning ) at construction when the cost matrix has no terms, or its terms cancel to exactly zero — such a metric always evaluates to 0.0 regardless of its parameters. Metric now warns when called with a parameter its cost matrix does not use, instead of silently ignoring it — catching a typo'd keyword argument. sample_weight and strategy-specific extras (e.g. Savings ' baseline ) are exempt. Multi-letter symbols now render upright in the LaTeX representations of CostMatrix and Metric , so a product such as clv * r reads as two variables rather than as one named clvr . Greek names such as gamma are unaffected. MaxProfit with integration_method='auto' now uses quasi-Monte Carlo for any number of stochastic variables whose distributions can be sampled, rather than only above two. Two stochastic variables used to go to nested quadrature. Pass random_state for a result reproducible across Metric instances; repeated calls on one instance were already identical. Deterministic MaxProfit metrics (a profit function polynomial in the stochastic variable) no longer compute the ROC convex hull, and evaluate the profit function vectorized over all operating points instead of in a Python loop. Quasi-Monte Carlo integration now covers eleven more distributions: BoundedPareto , Dagum , ExponentialPower (not published in SymPy's own documentation, so no link is possible), Frechet , Gompertz , LogLogistic , RaisedCosine , Rayleigh , Reciprocal , Weibull and WignerSemicircle . These previously fell through to plain Monte Carlo, which is around a thousand times less accurate for the same sampling budget. optimal_rate and optimal_threshold now always compute the exact EMP when one stochastic variable is present. MaxProfit accepts profit functions of any shape in the stochastic variable. Previously a cost matrix using exp , log or a square root raised PolynomialError from inside SymPy when the Metric was constructed. check_input has been removed from every prebuilt metric that is now a Metric / MixtureMetric instance ( empc_score , mpc_score , empb_score

summary: Invasive plant species pose a significant threat to global biodiversity, particularly within protected areas. This study investigated the diversity, community structure and distribution of invasive plants in Margalla Hills National Park (MHNP), Pakistan, combining a systematic quadrat-based field survey with soil physicochemical analysis and a GIS/remote-sensing framework. Surveys were conducted along 300 m transects, with separate quadrats for trees (10 × 10 m), shrubs (5 × 5 m) and herbs (1 × 1 m). The survey yielded 26 growth-form records representing 24 taxonomically distinct invasive species. Ricinus communis and Annona squamosa were each recorded as both a tree and a shrub. Overall records comprised 12 tree, 8 shrub and 6 herb growth forms. Because quadrat areas differed among growth forms, density was standardized to individuals m⁻² for cross-form comparison, on which basis herbs were by far the densest (5.19 m⁻²), followed by shrubs (0.77 m⁻²) and trees (0.14 m⁻²). Within growth forms, Sophora japonica led the trees (26.54 individuals quadrat⁻¹), Tecoma stans the shrubs (20.90) and Silybum marianum the herbs (5.58). Herbs also recorded the highest mean cover (24.99 ± 6.61%). Across the park, Broussonetia papyrifera, Parthenium hysterophorus and Lantana camara were the most frequently recorded dominants. The invasive assemblage was most species-rich and diverse in the tree layer (Shannon–Wiener H ≈ 2.52) and least diverse in the herb layer (≈ 1.98), reflecting the broad suite of woody invaders established in the park and the sustained pressure this places on native woody communities. Soils were neutral to slightly acidic (pH 6.63–7.22) with low electrical conductivity (0.81 dS m⁻¹) and very low organic matter (0.13 ± 0.01%), conditions associated with hardy, disturbance-adapted invaders. These findings confirm active invasion across all growth forms and provide a spatially explicit baseline for targeted management and long-term monitoring of this protected Himalayan ecosystem.
title: Community structure, edaphic drivers and ecological impacts of invasive plant species in Margalla Hills National Park, Pakistan

summary: Hashing Is Not Retrieval is a prospectively frozen three-arm evaluation of context accumulation in small-model multi-agent code cartography. It compares three ways for an orchestrator to hand work to a worker: 1. FULL HISTORY — retransmit prior worker outputs. 2. OPAQUE REF — replace the previous output with an unretrievable SHA-256 digest. 3. RETRIEVED — resolve the digest through a tenant-scoped content-addressed store and inject the recovered bytes. All arms receive identical source-derived evidence. The apparatus measures the exact message content sent to workers and records token counts, model and provider identifiers, generation IDs, usage, cost, retries, and retrieval proofs. A five-task gate preceded a fixed 50-task controlled benchmark, followed by a separate state-required evaluation across 24 deterministic fixtures and a five-scale Medusa case study. Key result: in the controlled benchmark, RETRIEVED reduced paired peak context by 38.3% relative to FULL HISTORY. The state-required follow-up shows that opaque references fail when state must be recovered, while verified retrieval preserves substantially more structural information. This is bounded-context evidence for automatic orchestrator-resolved state passing inside a specific two-worker code-cartography harness — not a universal claim about autonomous memory, long-context capability, or reasoning quality. The release includes the corrected author-identified preprint, executable apparatus, frozen results, task fixtures, telemetry, and verification instructions. Version 1.0.2 supplies the curated, verifier-passing reproducibility archive. It supersedes the uncurated archive from version 1.0.1 and includes the exact pinned apparatus, state-required fixtures, frozen results, and archive verifier. Submission status: This preprint was submitted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Long Context Foundation Models (LCFM). LCFM is a non-archival workshop; this Zenodo record is a public preprint and does not indicate acceptance or publication. Workshop information: https://longcontextfm.github.io/ Research website: https://abdulmoizahmed.com/research Concept DOI (all versions): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22844754 License: CC BY 4.0.
title: Hashing Is Not Retrieval: A Three-Arm Study of Context Accumulation in Small-Model Code Cartography

summary: Code, result tables, and figures for a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) study in which instruments for coronary artery disease (CAD) were filtered by colocalization (coloc.abf, PPH4 ≥ 0.8) with brain cell-type-specific cis-eQTLs from single-nucleus transcriptomics of human cortex (Bryois et al., Nature Genetics 2022). Of 274 CAD lead loci, 32 colocalized with brain-cell eQTLs, yielding 32 cell-annotated instruments (excitatory neurons 12, pericytes 7 after palindrome exclusion, oligodendrocytes 5, astrocytes 3, microglia 2, inhibitory neurons 1, OPC 1) explaining 3.4–5.6% of CAD liability on the liability scale. Random-effects inverse-variance weighted estimates (with weighted median, MR-Egger, leave-one-out, Cochran's Q and I², MR-PRESSO-analog global permutation, outlier correction, and MR-Steiger sensitivity analyses) are provided for ischemic stroke (OR 1.335, 95% CI 1.189–1.498, p = 1.0e-6), any stroke (OR 1.309, p = 8.5e-7), Alzheimer's disease (proxy-inclusive, and a clinically diagnosed replication arm), and major depression (null negative control). Cell-type-stratified analyses attribute the stroke effect to neuronal and neurovascular-unit (pericyte) expression programs. Contents: full analysis pipeline (R 4.6 / Python 3.13), all derived result tables (instruments, colocalization posteriors, harmonized exposure–outcome pairs, primary and stratified MR, leave-one-out, Steiger), publication figures (SVG/PDF vector plus ≥300 dpi PNG), the manuscript (v1.7), supplementary tables S1–S8, and the completed STROBE-MR checklist. Raw GWAS summary statistics are not redistributed; all sources are public (GWAS Catalog accessions GCST90132315, GCST006908, GCST006906, GCST90027158, GCST007511, GCST005839; eQTL record 10.5281/zenodo.7276971) and every number needed to reproduce the tables and figures is included.
title: Cell-type-stratified Mendelian randomization implicates neuronal and neurovascular expression programs in the causal effect of coronary artery disease on stroke: analysis code, result tables, and figures

summary: The analytical dataset and full extraction provenance for a study of how the cross-validation splitting rule affects machine-learning performance reported on literature-compiled membrane data. 512 canonical CO2/N2 permeation measurements were read from 82 open-access studies published 2020-2026. Every value carries the page it was read from, a content hash, and the DOI of its source. An identical panel of models was evaluated under two splitting rules: cross-validation grouped by source study, and a random row split. Contents: dataset.csv, the analytical dataset of 512 rows; observations.csv, pre-canonicalisation observations; citation_table.csv, every value attributed to its source DOI; fulltext_decisions.csv, the screening ledger with a reason for every decision; human_decisions.csv, the researcher's corrections; source_repairs.json, the sentence from the source justifying each repair; adjudication.json, contradictions between sources and how each was resolved; expansion_protocol.json, the corpus expansion protocol recorded before the run; rights_ledger.csv, rights_decisions.csv and rights_manifest.json, the release decision recorded for each study and what was withheld. No source PDF, rendered page image, or figure reproduced from a source is included. Each study is identified by DOI so that it can be retrieved from its publisher under that publisher's terms. Fourteen studies released their extracted values but not the short sentences quoted as evidence, because their licence could not be established or is not a Creative Commons licence; those sentences are marked as withheld in the files and listed in rights_manifest.json. All 512 rows are present, so the deposit reproduces the analysis reported in the manuscript. Version 1.0.1 adds the logged random audit: audit_draw.json (the sample, recorded before any row was inspected, with its seed), audit_log.jsonl (one verdict per row, each carrying the time it was given and the row's content hash) and audit_result.json (agreement and the error-rate bound). A random audit of 40 of the 512 accepted rows found 0 disagreements with the source page, bounding the error rate above by 7.2% (95% Clopper-Pearson). No data file changed between 1.0.0 and 1.0.1.
title: Machine learning for CO2/N2 separation performance across membrane material families: a grouped cross-validation study - analytical dataset and provenance

summary: Within the Complementarity-First and Reciprocal Internal Complementarity research program, we study the linear perturbations of the smooth massive magnetic core constructed in the companion paper. The host is a supplied flat-space SU(2) Yang–Mills theory with one adjoint scalar, unit magnetic degree, and equal scalar and vector masses. The action and physical scales are not derived from reciprocity. Starting from the full Cartesian second variation and linear Gauss constraint, we organize the physical angular sectors without excluding translations, boundary phase, or neutral radiation. A positive whole-half-line comparison gives a 4/25 lower bound in the two-profile magnetic radial sector. The separate spherical electric-flux operator has a positive but unquantified gap after charge and boundary data are separated. Explicit first-nonradial matrices, a compact-annulus Schur reduction, symbolic-angular-momentum higher matrices, and rational core certificates give all-angular nonnegativity conditional on the stated background and sufficient certificate predicates. The framed kernel consists of three translations and one phase tangent. In a covariant derivative-and-mass completion, a compact-remainder argument gives coercivity modulo this collective space with an unquantified positive constant. The kinetic wave operator nevertheless has essential spectrum [0,∞): exactly Gauss-dressed photon packets retain the zero threshold. An exact translation–photon overlap constructs fields orthogonal to the full kernel in L2 whose energy tends to zero while their local core tends to a nonzero translation. Thus energy-space or local-moment projection, not ordinary L2 orthogonality, is required for the stated coercivity. The result is a conditional linear sign, kernel, and norm-control theorem, not nonlinear orbital stability, decay, a numerical mode spectrum, or a monopole population prediction.
tags: Complementarity-First; Reciprocal Internal Complementarity; magnetic monopole; Yang–Mills– Higgs Hessian; coercivity; collective modes; photon continuum; computer-assisted proof; Lean.

summary: Topic models, in particular Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), have been adapted to hyperspectral imagery (HSI) as a route to interpretable spectral mixtures: each spectral unit (canonically a pixel) becomes a document of quantised band-frequency tokens and the inferred topic-word distributions act as non-negative basis spectra. Yet the dominant evaluation criterion remains downstream classification accuracy, an accuracy-only view that is silent on whether the basis is reproducible, band-robust, calibrated, or actually outperforms standard linear baselines. We propose and instantiate a twelve-axis evaluation framework for LDA-style topic models on HSI that quantifies, on the same set of benchmarks: (F-1) classification macro-F1 compared across five method families (paired differences and a hierarchical Bayesian model), (F-2) topic-word coherence (c_v, c_NPMI, U-Mass), (F-3) seed stability for both LDA and two neural variants (ProdLDA, ETM), (F-4) capacity sensitivity across K in {4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16}, (F-5) band-mask robustness, (F-6) cross-method clustering agreement (LDA vs Felzenszwalb, SLIC, patches, pixels), (F-7) topic-label coupling via P(L | t) entropy and KL, (F-8) per-topic Hungarian-aligned identity tracking, (F-9) HIDSAG cross-preprocessing stability, (F-10) cross-scene topic transfer, (F-11) rate-distortion of the topic representation, and (F-12) external alignment of the topics with a spectral library and a method-rank cross-comparison. We apply the framework to six standard HSI benchmarks (Indian Pines, Salinas, Salinas-A, Pavia University, Kennedy Space Center, Botswana) and five subsets of the HIDSAG mineralogical database (GEOMET, MINERAL1, MINERAL2, GEOCHEM, PORPHYRY). The framework yields three findings that the accuracy-only view does not surface. First, on the labelled scenes the topic-routed soft classifier, which routes the raw spectrum to per-topic logistic experts, matches the raw-spectrum logistic baseline in macro-F1 (0.915 against 0.910, a paired difference of 0.005), while a logistic regression on the topic proportions theta alone trails the baseline by 0.325: the topics add an interpretable routing to the raw spectrum but do not replace it. Second, on Salinas-A under the SWIR-only band mask the paired ARI between canonical and masked dominant-topic maps reaches 0.766, while on Kennedy Space Center under every mask, and on Botswana under the SWIR mask, the same paired ARI collapses to approximately 0.01, separating scenes on which an interpretability claim is band-robust from scenes on which it is not. Third, the theta-only deficit holds on HIDSAG: over its nineteen mineralogical targets the topic-logistic classifier trails raw-logistic by 0.268 macro-F1 (lower on 18 of 19 targets), contrary to the prima-facie expectation that mineralogical mixtures favour topic decomposition over the raw spectrum. We release 3895 deterministic derived artefacts (449 MB), the builder source, the FastAPI backend, the React frontend, and a 109-endpoint test harness as a public, MIT-licensed reproducibility package. Code and derived artefacts: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_LDA_HSI . Interactive web application: https://lda-hsi.fasl-work.com . Manuscript sources: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_LDA_HSI_Paper . Funding: The Advanced Mining Technology Center (AMTC) Basal project (ANID/PIA Project AFB220002) and ANID FONDECYT Postdoctorado 3220094.
title: Beyond Accuracy: A Multi-Axis Evaluation Framework for Interpretable Topic Models on Hyperspectral Imagery

summary: The COVID-19 pandemic altered human mobility and natural-resource management, potentially affecting wildlife in rural landscapes where conservation and livestock production coexist. This work evaluated temporal variation in mammal detections in the Bienes Comunales Santa Cruz Nuevo Wildlife Management Unit, Puebla, Mexico, using camera-trap data from two pre-pandemic surveys (2018 and 2019) and a post-restriction survey (2022). Sampling comprised 39 station-years and 3,193.31 effective camera-days. The work compared encounter rates, station-level occurrence, and observed and estimated species richness among years, and also examined associations between wild mammals, domestic animals, human activity, altitude, and vegetation attributes. Species richness varied substantially among years: 14 species were recorded in 2018, nine in 2019, and 11 in 2022. Chao2 estimates and station-based rarefaction supported this interannual variability rather than a consistent directional change. Gray fox ( Urocyon cinereoargenteus ) detections declined significantly during the post-restriction survey relative to the pre-pandemic baseline (rate ratio = 0.280, 95% CI = 0.129–0.604, FDR-adjusted q = 0.025). Other species showed uncertain or non-estimable temporal effects because of sparse detections or complete zeros. Raccoon detections were negatively associated with altitude, whereas gray fox and coyote detections were associated with livestock occurrence. These findings demonstrate species-specific temporal responses and emphasize that nondetection or nonsignificant results do not necessarily indicate ecological stability. Although the observed changes coincided with the COVID-19 period, they cannot be attributed exclusively to pandemic restrictions because the year also represented climatic, ecological, and management variation.
title: Fauna–Vegetation correlations and relative abundance in a fragmented landscape of Southwest Mexico: Pre- and Post-COVID-19 analysis

summary: MATLAB implementation, per-item numeric results and figure code for the study "Dissociating Prompt Quality from Response Compliance in Automated Prompt-Engineering Assessment". A four-agent evaluator running on a locally hosted Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct judge scores each prompt as an artifact before any response exists, then scores the resulting response twice on identical items: once against criteria extracted from that prompt, and once against a fixed rubric that never sees it. Verifiable constraints are checked with the IFEval reference implementation rather than model-generated labels. The whole pipeline runs on consumer CPU hardware with no external API calls. Contents: src/ the MATLAB agents and run scripts; scripts/ the IFEval verifier and the figure code; data/ a SHA-256 manifest of all 4,275 benchmark prompts and the filtered IFEval subset; results/ per-item results for the main run (n = 500) and the ablation (n = 120), the construct-validation output and the IFEval verification output. Corpus not redistributed. No prompt or response text from LMSYS-Chat-1M or WildChat-1M is included; the LMSYS agreement prohibits transfer to third parties and WildChat-1M carries flow-down obligations under the AI2 ImpACT licence. Prompts appear only as SHA-256 hashes, so an independently rebuilt corpus can be verified as identical to the one used here. The IFEval subset is included in full under Apache-2.0.
title: Dissociating Prompt Quality from Response Compliance in Automated Prompt-Engineering Assessment: evaluator, results and figure code

summary: Extended reasoning can increase response time and computational cost without improving an answer. Models may revisit unproductive steps or build further reasoning on an earlier mistake. This study evaluates whether Jev, a probabilistic decision maker, can provide an inexpensive error signal to help decide when additional reasoning is needed. We compare Jev with GPT-5.6 Luna on generated ordering and logic-grid puzzles and on the official released ZebraLogic test set. The generated questions are four-choice items with one correct answer among four. The official test set is used open-ended: Luna produces the full grid, Jev checks it without the solution key, and Luna may revise once when Jev does not judge the answer consistent. On the generated multiple-choice problems, Jev is 5 to 60 percentage points more accurate than Luna with reasoning disabled, at lower measured API cost, and every observed top-choice disagreement identifies a Luna error. On a stratified sample of 200 official ZebraLogic puzzles, exact-grid accuracy rises from 41.0% with reasoning disabled to 90.5% with high-effort reasoning. A revision pass adds two points in both settings, but a revision-only control shows the gain comes from the extra attempt, not from Jev's information: on the answers Jev flags, a plain second look is at least as accurate as the Jev-informed revision (16 versus 13 correct without reasoning, and 70 versus 70 at high effort). Jev detects 93% of the weak reasoner's errors with 92% precision, but only 10% of its high-effort flags identify errors. These results motivate using Jev or similar decision models in a model harness: software that controls when to continue, reconsider, retrieve evidence, or allocate more reasoning. An early check could help avoid spending further computation on a mistaken line of reasoning. The experiments measure checking of final answers, however, and do not measure reductions in hallucination or repetitive reasoning inside a harness. On the official benchmark, extra reasoning accounts for most of the accuracy, and the checker's information does not improve on a second attempt. Larger studies with balanced answer positions, selective triggers, and step-level feedback are needed to test whether checking improves accuracy or reduces total cost.
title: Evaluating Jev for Cost-Effective Candidate Verification: An Exploratory Study

summary: Certificate archive for "A computer-assisted lower bound for Landau's constant" (Frank Wikström, Lund University). This archive is the computer-assisted part of the proof of the lower bounds B_inf > 0.51 for the locally univalent Bloch constant and L > 0.51 for Landau's constant, improving the bound 1/2 + 2·10^-8 of Chen and Shiba (2004). The manuscript is distributed separately and is not part of the archive. The certified statement is that each of the 1179 boxes of a finite cover of the normalized logarithmic coefficient body admits a schlicht disc of radius greater than 0.51. The smallest certified radius over the cover is [0.5100305329006052049176652 ± 4.18e-26], obtained with Arb ball arithmetic at 80 decimal digits. Contents (3.2 GB, single top-level folder landau-certificate-051/): - the cover manifest landau-cover-split-051-caps.json: the binary tree with exact dyadic splits, contractions and LP caps with their dual vectors, the 776 sources with SHA-256 digests, and the exact shift of every leaf; - the 776 certificate sources: cut descriptors, radial grids, angular arcs, sparse non-negative dual multipliers and curvature duals; - the reference verification run: twelve shard logs with the enclosure of every leaf, their transcripts, and the aggregation output; - the snapshot of the checker that produced those logs, with a SHA-256 inventory and a provenance record binding the logs to the manifest and the checker; - rejection tests, the search scripts that built the manifest from the stored sources, a pinned environment (CPython 3.12, python-flint 0.9.0, numpy 2.5.1, scipy 1.18.0), and the expected output of every command. The checker reconstructs every inequality from the stored exact data and does not call a linear programming solver or trust any stored numerical value; the floating-point search that found the multipliers is included for reuse but is not part of the proof. README.md gives three commands: aggregate the archived shard logs (about half a minute), verify a single leaf (a few minutes), and rerun the complete verification (about two hours on twelve cores). Released under the MIT License. Version 1.0.0.
title: Certificate archive for: A computer-assisted lower bound for Landau's constant

summary: This dataset provides a curated and reproducible compilation of data used to analyze long-term trends in external-cause mortality in Ecuador from 1990 through 2024. The primary data sources are official mortality statistics and population estimates and projections published by Ecuador’s National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos, INEC). The dataset includes annual mortality counts and population-based indicators for major external-cause categories, including land transport injuries, other transport accidents and accidental injuries, suicide, homicide, events of undetermined intent, and other external causes. Where available, the data are organized by calendar year, sex, age or age group, geographic unit, ICD classification, and cause of death. Population denominators, crude mortality rates, confidence intervals, absolute and relative changes, mortality composition measures, sex-specific rate ratios, and variables used in the statistical analyses are documented separately from the original source data. The repository also contains information used to support the reproducibility of the associated scientific study, including analytical datasets, variable definitions, ICD harmonization information, population denominators, model-related variables, sensitivity-analysis data, quality-control documentation, data provenance, and records of differences identified between historical editions of INEC statistical tables. Hospital discharge datasets reviewed during data curation are documented at the variable and source level. Individual-level hospital discharge microdata are not included in the public dissemination package when their inclusion could create unnecessary privacy or re-identification risks. Original source information is kept distinct from derived variables and researcher-calculated indicators to preserve full provenance and auditability. The package follows FAIR data principles and includes machine-readable CSV files together with the original curated Excel database, a data dictionary, methodology documentation, provenance and transformation records, quality-control information, ethics and privacy considerations, citation metadata, licensing information, and version history. No missing values were imputed solely for publication, and no undocumented assumptions were used to generate unavailable data. Values for recent years should be interpreted according to the provisional or revised status indicated by the original INEC sources. This dataset is intended to support reproducibility, secondary epidemiological analyses, public health surveillance, methodological review, and research on injuries, violence, suicide, homicide, road traffic mortality, and other external causes of death in Ecuador.
title: Ecuador External-Cause Mortality, Population Denominators, and Reproducibility Dataset, 1990–2024

summary: This dataset provides source records, recalculated supplementary tables, and reduced principal component analyses for woody crown hydraulic networks (WCHNs) from Caatinga and Cerrado vegetation in Brazil. It accompanies a critical review of the WCHN framework but is documented so that the dataset can be understood and reused independently of that manuscript. The deposit contains 13 files: three source spreadsheets, six recalculated or additional supplementary tables, one analytical PCA workbook, two PCA figures, and a comprehensive README. The source spreadsheets comprise 14 individuals of Cenostigma pyramidale classified into three WCHN size classes; ten additional Caatinga species represented by one WCHN each; and 15 Cerrado species represented by five WCHNs per species, totaling 75 networks. These spreadsheets preserve the WCHN diagrams, decomposition and topology records, original equations, and property values used in the source study. The supplementary tables recalculate symmetry (SYM), complexity (COM), and vulnerability (VUL) using revised equations. Revised SYM is expressed as the inverse coefficient of variation of IN–FN topological distances, SYM = 1/CV = μ/σ. Revised COM is COM = ΣNO × CV, making explicit the identity COM × SYM = ΣNO. Revised VUL excludes the initial node from the attackable set while preserving it as the root of the network, giving an attackable set of ΣNO − 1 nodes. Results are provided for C. pyramidale size classes, Caatinga species, Cerrado species, and phenological groups, as well as a comparison between Caatinga and Cerrado vegetation. The deposit also includes recalculated PERMANOVAs for the deciduous, semideciduous, and evergreen Cerrado groups. For recalculated property blocks, the analyses use species means, Bray–Curtis distances, and an exact enumeration of all 252 possible allocations of five species to each of two groups. An additional reduced-set PERMANOVA excludes the algebraically dependent properties COM and SHA. The DE–EV contrast was consistently the strongest pairwise differentiation, although its significance after correction for multiple comparisons depended on the property set analyzed. Separate reduced PCAs were performed for Caatinga and Cerrado using NAV, revised VUL, LAT, BAS, and PTP, without prior transformation and based on correlation matrices. The Caatinga analysis contains 24 WCHNs representing 11 species; its first two axes explain 91.1% of the total variance. The primary Cerrado analysis contains 74 complete cases from 15 species and excludes one network with an undefined BAS value; its first two axes explain 89.0% of the variance. A sensitivity analysis retaining all 75 Cerrado WCHNs by substituting the column mean for the single undefined BAS value produced essentially the same ordination structure. In both vegetation types, PC1 contrasts vulnerability with navigability, basitony, and potential topological plasticity, whereas PC2 is dominated by laterality. These convergent ordination structures identify two complementary dimensions of WCHN organization but describe covariance rather than causal relationships. The recalculated tables and reduced PCAs assess the topological component of the WCHN framework. They do not directly measure crown hydraulic resistance, xylem P₅₀, hydraulic safety margins, or causal effects on attained tree height. The dataset therefore provides comparative topological evidence and tests the framework’s internal structure, rather than fully validating hydraulic function mechanistically. The original analyses and table numbering are reported in Prado and Trovão (2023), Ecological Modelling , 481, 110345, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2023.110345 . Related stochastic WCHN data and computational experiments are available separately at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21839645 .
title: Recalculated woody crown hydraulic network properties and reduced principal component analyses of Caatinga and Cerrado trees

summary: This technical note investigates whether operator-relative noncentrality can predict the relative empirical power of complementary localized scan statistics in correlated spectra. The motivating real-data benchmark compares BABAR and BESIII measurements of the e⁺e⁻ → π⁺π⁻ cross section in the ρ-resonance region on a common 5 MeV grid from 0.600 to 0.880 GeV. The real-data comparison remains negative, with no statistically supported localized shape tension identified. The methodological study compares a coherent-yield scan with a covariance-profiled shape scan and defines the frozen coordinate Θ = log(ES/EY), where ES and EY represent maximum local operator-accessible signal strengths. An archival confirmatory replication used 50,000 null calibration draws per covariance environment, 15,000 independent null-validation draws per environment, 1,440 signal/covariance conditions, and 576,000 injected pseudoexperiments. Θ predicted which scan had greater empirical power with pooled AUC 0.9820 and mean leave-one-covariance-environment-out AUC 0.9740; its correlation with the empirical power difference was 0.9185. Independent Type-I error estimates ranged from 0.0466 to 0.0540. The results support operator-relative noncentrality as a useful empirical coordinate for complementary globally calibrated scans within the tested benchmark. The underlying ingredients, including Gaussian noncentrality, covariance-weighted subspace detection, quadratic scanning, and Monte Carlo calibration, are established; the contribution is a reproducible computational synthesis and controlled characterization rather than a claim of a new general statistical law
title: Operator-Relative Noncentrality in Localized Correlated-Spectrum Scans: A BABAR–BESIII Benchmark
