summary: Supporting material for the manuscript "Subacute oral glyphosate impairs testicular function in male mice (Mus musculus): a threshold-anchored dose-response study of steroidogenesis, sperm quality, redox balance and spermatogenic histopathology" (Elbeeh, Filfilan, Filfilan and Filfilan), submitted to Drug and Chemical Toxicology (Taylor & Francis). Forty adult male Swiss albino (ICR) mice, 8-10 weeks old and 22.1-25.5 g at allocation, received vehicle (distilled water) or technical-grade glyphosate at 10, 50 or 100 mg/kg/day by oral gavage for 28 days, n = 10 per group. The dose range brackets the regulatory no-observed-adverse-effect level of approximately 50 mg/kg/day. Endpoints measured in the same 40 animals: body and testis weight; serum testosterone, LH and FSH; epididymal sperm concentration, progressive motility, viability and morphology; testicular malondialdehyde, reduced glutathione, superoxide dismutase and catalase; and testis histopathology stained with haematoxylin-eosin and with periodic acid-Schiff, assessed by the Johnsen tubular-maturation score and by measurement of seminiferous tubule diameter, germinal epithelial height and graded lesion severity. Sections were digitised on a Philips UltraFast Scanner at the x20 level (0.5 micrometres per pixel) and reviewed in the Philips PathologySuite viewer; morphometry was performed in ImageJ v1.54 with semi-automated annotation in QuPath v0.4.3 on fields exported at the native scan resolution. Contents: S1, the manufacturer's Certificate of Analysis for the test article (Sigma-Aldrich 337757, lot MKCZ1523, purity at least 96 per cent, CAS 1071-83-6); S2, analytical kits, instruments, assay conditions and intra- and inter-assay coefficients of variation; S3, the analysis and figure-plotting code; S4, the complete per-animal dataset underlying every figure and table; S5, the benchmark-dose model set with BMD and BMDL10 values; Supplementary Figure S6 with its caption, showing the histomorphometry and graded lesion scores of Table 4 with individual animal values overlaid; S7, the completed ARRIVE 2.0 checklist; S8, the full statistical record for all 30 endpoints (Shapiro-Wilk and Levene checks, the test applied, post-hoc comparisons, effect sizes, Benjamini-Hochberg q values, Jonckheere-Terpstra trend statistics, dose-response correlations and benchmark-dose fits) together with the group mean, SEM and n behind every plotted point; and S9, the unmodified field exported from the whole-slide image behind each panel of Figures 4 and 5, both plates before the arrows were drawn, a manifest of exactly what was done to each image, and checksums. README.md gives the full manifest. Every value reported in the manuscript can be recomputed from S4 using the code in S3. Statistics: continuous endpoints were compared by Welch's ANOVA with the Games-Howell post-hoc test; ordinal lesion grades by the Kruskal-Wallis test with Holm-adjusted Dunn's post-hoc test; monotonic trend by the Jonckheere-Terpstra test; and the endpoint family was controlled at a false-discovery rate of 5 per cent (Benjamini-Hochberg). The Johnsen tubular-maturation score was nominated in advance as the primary endpoint; every other endpoint is secondary. Ethics: all procedures were approved by the Bioethics Committee of Umm Al-Qura University, Makkah, Saudi Arabia (approval no. HAPO-02-K-012-2025-04-2781) and were conducted in accordance with the ARRIVE 2.0 guidelines. These 40 animals also support the cardiotoxicity, neurotoxicity and immunotoxicity arms of the same programme, which are reported separately under the same approval number. Licensed CC BY 4.0. Version 2.0.0 adds S8 and S9, replaces S3 with a copy that also carries requirements.txt, a README and the benchmark-dose output table, and replaces the Supplementary Figure S6 image with a copy from which a non-standard private PNG chunk, added in transit and carrying no image information, has been removed. No reported value changed between versions 1.
title: Supplementary data and analysis code for: Subacute oral glyphosate impairs testicular function in male mice (Mus musculus)

summary: Nearly 90% of drugs entering clinical development ultimately fail, despite billions of dollars in investment. Pharmaceutical companies therefore rely on clinical development planning (CDP) and probability of technical and regulatory success assessment to anticipate development risks, yet these decisions remain labor-intensive and subjective, requiring experts across clinical science, statistics, regulatory affairs, and competitive intelligence to jointly acquire, synthesize, and reason over heterogeneous evidence. Here, we introduce TrialAtlas, a memory-augmented multi-agent research organization for CDP that mirrors this collaborative process by coordinating specialized agents for literature synthesis, competitive trial intelligence, regulatory precedent analysis, and integrated reasoning over trial design and development risk. TrialAtlas further learns from historical clinical trials and regulatory outcomes, including prior New Drug Applications (NDAs), to ground its decisions in accumulated development experience. To evaluate these capabilities in an authentic regulatory setting, we introduce TrialAtlasBench, constructed from 291 FDA Complete Response Letters and spanning three practical tasks: detecting trial design deficiencies, recommending actionable design improvements, and predicting technical and regulatory success. TrialAtlas achieves an F1 score of 50.0% for deficiency detection, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.1 points, and reaches 85.3% balanced accuracy and 84.7% F1 for prediction of technical and regulatory success, improving over the best baselines by 6.7 points in balanced accuracy and 12.0 points in Cohen's kappa. In expert evaluation, 86.4% of TrialAtlas-generated concerns were judged valid, compared with 83.1% for OpenAI DeepResearch and 59.3% for Gemini DeepResearch.
title: TrialAtlas: Multi-Agent Research Organization for Clinical Trial Design and Optimization

summary: Field robotics missions often require physical samples to be returned to laboratories for analysis, making path planning inherently load-aware and order-dependent as accumulated samples increase payload and traversal energy costs. In single-robot Load-Aware Informative Path Planning (LIPP), this rigidly couples sensing with hauling: a solitary robot must transport every collected sample, forcing frequent depot returns that severely restrict its spatial coverage. Heterogeneous multi-robot teams can overcome this bottleneck by dividing labor---enabling high-precision samplers to collect while high-capacity carriers handle transport. However, this introduces a complex coordination challenge regarding when, where, what, and to whom handoffs should occur on top of the LIPP problem. To address this tightly coupled problem, we introduce Multi-Agent LIPP (MA-LIPP), which enables teams to cooperate through asynchronous "dead drops," allowing one robot to deposit samples for another to retrieve later without requiring synchronous rendezvous. We formulate MA-LIPP as an exact Mixed-Integer Quadratic Program (MIQP) alongside a scalable Pairwise Large-Neighborhood Search (LNS) heuristic for complex real-world applications. The heuristic matches exact optima in $95.5\%$ of certified cases and reduces weighted posterior variance by $16.1$--$19.8\%$ relative to a sequential baseline on larger instances of up to 12 robots, providing a robust framework for cooperative physical-sampling missions.
title: MA-LIPP: Cooperative Multi-Agent Load-Aware Informative Path Planning for Heterogeneous Robot Teams

summary: Blind and low-vision users often need to locate a specific personal object rather than an arbitrary instance of the same category. The task calls for a robot that can move through the space and reach viewpoints the user cannot, and for an accessible interface where the user says which object is meant and learns whether the right one was found. We present RoboFind, a multi-agent framework in which a smartphone teaches the target and a quadruped robot carries out the search. A Target Teaching Agent converts guided smartphone recordings into a semantic target profile and a reusable multi-view reference bank through an accessible capture flow with AR guidance, speech and haptic feedback, and screen-reader support, so later missions refer to a stored object without repeating the teaching process. At runtime, a Navigation Agent explores the environment and proposes candidate targets, a Verification Agent checks each candidate against the stored references, and a Coordination and Recovery Agent completes the mission or triggers recovery and continued search. Across 32 real-robot missions, RoboFind reaches 85.0% success against 25.0% for a reconstructed sequential first-stop baseline over 20 trials with ten targets, and reduces false success from 75.0% to 5.0%. On six shared targets it succeeds in 10/12 trials, against 5/12 for 12 independently executed GPT-6 Astra-only trials. These results show that the multi-agent design fits the demands of personalized object search, where verifying object identity before declaring completion is what makes the outcome something a user can rely on.
title: RoboFind: Multi-Agent Personalized Object Search for People Who Are Blind or Have Low Vision

summary: This paper asks what would be required to create a credible public registry of serious AI incidents. It compares mandatory and voluntary ledgers in transportation, medicine, product safety, and cybersecurity, then analyzes incentives that produce under-reporting, duplication, and denominator gaps. A proposed registry design separates event intake from causal adjudication and preserves revisions and provenance. The paper is a governance synthesis based on public materials; it does not claim that existing incident databases provide complete counts of AI harms.
title: The Incident Registry Void

summary: This paper examines model distillation as both a technical compression method and a channel through which capabilities, errors, and provenance constraints may propagate across model generations. It separates teacher-student training evidence from broader claims about market structure and governance, and compares rationale distillation, imitation, synthetic supervision, and recursive training. The paper argues for explicit lineage records and evaluation at each transfer step. It is a synthesis of published results and public records, not a new model-training experiment.
title: The Distillation Chain

summary: This paper develops a reliability framework for multi-step AI agents. It begins with the conditional multiplication rule for end-to-end success, then examines how correlated errors, persistent state, retries, verification, human review, and irreversible actions alter operational reliability. The analysis distinguishes bounded benchmark success from dependable delegation and uses published agent and robotics evaluations to show why chain length and verification cost matter. Its contribution is conceptual and arithmetic: it does not estimate a universal per-step failure rate, and its numerical examples should be read as sensitivity calculations rather than forecasts.
title: The Reliability Multiplication Law

summary: This archive accompanies the article "A prediction market reacts sooner to more obvious home runs, without a detectable rise in the spread of its reaction times" (Ivailo Petrov, Western University). It contains the analysis code, the reaction detector and the scripts that retrieve the public inputs. It also contains the event-level analysis file for the 549 home runs, SHA-256 hashes of every input file analysed, and the dated analysis plan written before the tests were run. Every number reported in the article is printed by a script in the code folder. Most start from the shipped event-level file. Two groups of numbers need inputs that are not redistributed: the anticipatory events, and the calibration of the obviousness model. The scripts that retrieve and rebuild those inputs are included. Raw exchange trade records are not included, because the exchange's data terms do not permit redistributing archived data sets. See README.md for the full guide.
title: Replication code and data for "A prediction market reacts sooner to more obvious home runs, without a detectable rise in the spread of its reaction times"

summary: REPRO specifies a benchmark for autonomous CVE validation from a bounded input: a public advisory and a vulnerable repository revision. An agent must reconstruct the environment, produce a minimal non-weaponized trigger, and establish a designated security effect under external oracles. The benchmark separates environment build, surface reachability, trigger validity, effect proof, repeatability, and differential validation against a fixed revision. It does not reward persistence, stealth, post-exploitation, or damage. This study protocol defines tasks, oracles, scoring, baselines, statistical analysis, containment, disclosure, and artifact review; comparative findings require construction and execution of the benchmark.
title: REPRO Study Protocol for Autonomous CVE Validation

summary: AUTHZBENCH specifies a benchmark in which every agent task carries an executable authority manifest covering required, permitted, forbidden, approval-gated, and budgeted effects. The environment records canonical state transitions rather than relying on an evaluator model to infer violations from text. Results jointly report task success, authority-violation incidence, severity, exposure opportunity, time-to-first violation, and unnecessary authority use. Clean, adversarial, ambiguous, and planner-compromise tracks distinguish ordinary reliability from susceptibility to untrusted content and from enforcement-layer strength. This study protocol defines policy semantics, task construction, attack taxonomy, metrics, statistical analysis, governance, and reproducibility requirements; comparative claims require construction and execution of the benchmark.
title: AUTHZBENCH Study Protocol for Evaluating Whether Autonomous Agents Stay Within Delegated Authority

summary: Medicine-level dataset and complete R analysis code for the retrospective cohort study Authorised in Europe, Awaited in Bulgaria: A Time-to-Event Analysis of Where the 3.9-Year Delay to Oncology Medicine Reimbursement Accrues (Department of Social Medicine and Public Health, Medical University of Plovdiv, Bulgaria). The dataset links 294 centrally authorised oncology medicinal products from the European Medicines Agency's public medicine data (marketing authorisation date and status, ATC code, therapeutic area, marketing authorisation holder, and the new active substance, generic, biosimilar, orphan, conditional approval, accelerated assessment, PRIME and advanced therapy designations) to the Bulgarian reimbursement record of the National Council on Prices and Reimbursement of Medicinal Products: the start and end dates and outcome of the published HTA procedure, and the first appearance of each product in 130 dated monthly snapshots of Annex 2 of the Positive Drug List (16 October 2015 to 2 July 2026), with the provenance of each date. The primary cohort of the article is the 189 medicines authorised from 16 October 2015. The unit of observation is the medicinal product; no personal data are involved. The code reproduces every estimate, table and figure of the article and its supplement: Kaplan-Meier cumulative probabilities of reimbursement, decomposition of the interval into company submission and HTA assessment phases, Cox models stratified by product type (with robust, new-active-substance-only and advanced-therapy-excluded sensitivity fits), competing-risk and alternative-endpoint sensitivity analyses. See README.md and codebook.md.
title: Time from EMA marketing authorisation to reimbursement in Bulgaria for 294 centrally authorised oncology medicines, 2005-2026: medicine-level dataset and analysis code

summary: This release provides the data and code supporting a simulation-only study of reference-assisted radiofrequency fracture sensing under anatomical domain shift. It includes 5,580 corrected noise-free RF acquisitions, 356,400 feature rows from 20 independent noise repetitions, model predictions, calibration outputs and paired H2 statistical analyses. MATLAB and Python source code, fixed analysis specifications, figure-generation code and provenance records are included. The materials support reproducible evaluation of independent healthy references and source-locked decision thresholds across five idealised anatomical locations. All data are simulated and do not establish clinical diagnostic accuracy.
title: Data and Code for Machine Learning Based Reference Assisted Signal Recovery Under Anatomical Domain Shift in Simulated Radiofrequency Fracture Sensing

summary: Supplementary data and code accompanying the manuscript “An Evidence-Chain Provenance Framework for Tracing the Overseas Circulation of Oracle Bones: A GIS-Based Approach”. This package provides materials for editors and referees to check the study’s methods and results. It includes: (i) the Tier A–D evidence-classification coding scheme; (ii) circulation-pathway tables and CSV files aligned with Tables 1–3; (iii) record-level evidence codes underlying Fig. 6; (iv) an English evidence-ledger digest; (v) a bilingual Chinese–English concordance of cited Chinese-language sources and personal names; (vi) location notes for GIS visualizations; (vii) Python scripts used to generate Figs. 1–6; (viii) finished figure PNGs matching the manuscript; and (ix) a public-domain Natural Earth basemap for re-running Fig. 5. The study synthesizes published historical sources, museum catalogues, and publicly disclosed institutional records. No new laboratory, survey, or interview datasets were generated. Author-generated materials are shared under CC BY 4.0; copyrighted verbatim text of published sources is cited but not reproduced in full. Natural Earth data are public domain.
title: Supplementary for "An Evidence-Chain Provenance Framework for Tracing the Overseas Circulation of Oracle Bones: A GIS-Based Approach"

summary: We introduce the M_R family of logarithmically weighted prime series as a Gaussian regularization of the prime Alpha family. The paper develops its joint holomorphy, exact differential hierarchy, vertical heat equation, Gaussian semigroup, Mellin and Laplace transforms, positivity properties, moment inequalities, almost periodicity, annular value geometry, zero-free regions, thermal asymptotics, and spectral reconstruction of the primes. A central result associates asymptotic vertical zero chains with consecutive prime pairs and proves that the slope and spacing of each chain recover the pair that generates it. The paper also develops a sequential limiting measure of zeros, zero–cumulant identities, additive and multiplicative arithmetic companions, operator-trace and Fredholm-determinant representations, and a multiscale thermal reflection framework. A selected algebraic, geometric, differential, and local two-term core was independently formalized and verified in Lean 4.12.0 with Mathlib. The formalization is partial and does not yet cover the infinite prime tail, the Rouché transfer argument, the complete asymptotic localization of the zeros, or the planar limiting-measure theorem. The verified Lean package is available as related software at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21581767. The manuscript does not claim to prove the Riemann hypothesis, Goldbach’s conjecture, or any other classical open problem. It presents the definitions, proofs, computational evidence, limitations, and open questions required for independent mathematical examination.
title: The M_R Family: Gaussian Regularization of the Prime Alpha Family, Geometry of Zeros, Arithmetic Structure, and Thermal Laws

Its central question is how the zeros of the Riemann zeta function can be studied through explicitly constructed arithmetic cohomology, spectral actions and quantitative metric estimates. The collection also retains the related heat-flow, arithmetic-trace, fluid, complexity and thermal-geometry investigations from which parts of this programme developed. What the collection contains Split-Zero coefficients, geometry and cohomology. The construction retains a ring's internal zero and a separate symbol for absence, so a zero element in a specified support fibre is not confused with an absent fibre. The papers construct coefficient maps, quotients, homology, finite spectral jets and their relation to the infinite theta quotient. Deligne's Weil II provides a motivating source for the cohomology–duality–weight-control programme; its finite-field theorem is not asserted to apply automatically to the Riemann zeta function. Read the cohomology and weight-control paper and the foundational objects and maps . Arithmetic theta sources and analytic control. summary: These datasets consist of median-binned (1-minute or 1-meter) fluorometric chlorophyll-a, fluorometric dissolved organic matter, and optical backscatter derived from FL* series instruments deployed by the National Science Foundation's Ocean Observatories Initiative (OOI) (https://oceanobservatories.org/) between April 2014 and August 2026. Glider data are not provided in this repository. It is strongly encouraged that the GliderDAC be used to access OOI glider datasets (https://gliders.ioos.us/) Datasets for instruments deployed at nominal depths have been organized into 1-minute median bins. Datasets for instruments deployed on profiling platforms have been organized into profiles with 1-meter median bins. Co-located and quality-assessed pressure, temperature, practical salinity, and density data are also included in each dataset, where applicable. Zip directories are oriented by the OOI subsite. e.g. CE02SHSM-FL contains all deployments of fluorometers deployed on the Coastal Endurance Oregon Shelf Mooring at all depths. Individual files are titled using the full OOI reference designator, the deployment number, the first and last day containing data in the file, and the file version number.  e.g. CE02SHSM-RID27-02-FLORTD000_D0010_20191020-20200113_V1.1.nc contains fluorometer data from Deployment 10 for the fluorometer located at 7M depth on the Coastal Endurance Oregon Shelf Surface Mooring. To identify data of interest, it is recommended that you review OOI array and instrument nomenclature (https://oceanobservatories.org/research-arrays/). To identify matchups with other OOI instruments, users should pay special attention the node and instrument reference designators. Generally, the first 2 or 3 characters of the node can be used to match up instruments. This does not work for Global deployments with instrument arrays deployed on the same node. In these instances, the last few characters of the instrument should be used to match up with the appropriate depth and other co-located instruments. WARNING : These datasets are intended to simplify access to a full deployment's worth of fluorometer data. No advanced reprocessing has been performed and I haven't looked at all of these datasets. In profiling datasets, the instrument offset between the fluorometer and the CTD pressure sensor has not been considered (which may be up to 20cm depending on the platform). Note that data may still contain spikes or trends. Some profiler datasets may have substantial gaps between depth cells or may have accidentally been split, so resampling profiles to a more coarse time bin may be a useful practice if high resolution profiles are not needed. For questions, issues, or if something looks odd, please email Ian Black (blackia@oregonstate.edu). Processing Steps 1) Data from all telemetry sources for a deployment are merged and duplicate entries are removed. 2) Data with QARTOD primary flags indicating failure (flag=4) are removed. 3) Data with human-in-the-loop annotations indicating failure (flag='fail') are removed. 4) Data are then binned.    - For 1-dimensional time-series, data are binned into 1-minute medians. The median absolute deviation and number of observations in the bin are also provided.    - For profiling time-series, data are binned by profile and into 1-meter medians, with the depth value indicating the center of the bin. Only upward profiles are provided. 5) In addition to fluorometer and scatterometer data, co-located CTD data are provided. These data were also processed following steps 1-3 and then linearly interpolated with a maximum gap of 6 hours for 1-dimensional datasets and 10 seconds for profiling datasets before the binning steps.   File Structure Each file consists of two groups. The root group is available on file read without specifying a group name and provides the primary science data. Category Variable Name Units Description Valid Min/Max dimension depth meters For Profile Datase
title: NSF-OOI Fluorometric Chlorophyll-a, FDOM, and Backscatter, 2014-2026

summary: Urban Agriculture as Green and Social Infrastructure: Persistence, Displacement, and Commons in São Paulo Replication package for the paper submitted to InfraCidades 2026 (FGV EAESP / SP Parcerias, São Paulo, Brazil). This repository contains the agent-based model, experimental protocols, statistical analyses, and figures underlying the article "Agricultura urbana como infraestrutura verde e social: persistência, deslocamento e bens comuns em São Paulo — evidências de uma modelagem baseada em agentes integrada no tempo" . What do we have here model/ — ABM (long-term agent-based model, v2.0): urban farmers facing land-market pressure and displacement under five protection policy scenarios (20-year horizon, monthly resolution). Includes the replication driver: deterministic seeds (CRC32), convergence analysis, and a reduced factorial experiment (tenure × subsidy × zoning). analysis/ — statistical tests in base R only: Kruskal–Wallis with ε² effect sizes, Mann–Whitney post-hoc with Holm correction, rank-biserial correlations, rank-based ANOVA for the factorial; plus the figure-generation script (Python, Portuguese labels). data/ — simulation outputs as reported in the article (1,050 runs in total: 150 + 300 + 300 + 300). outputs/ — figures (300 dpi, pt-BR) and statistical tables regenerated by the analysis scripts. Key results (as reported in the article) Protection gradient strictly monotonic: deterministic collapse under no protection (0% farmer retention in 20 years) vs. 80% retention under maximum protection; policy rankings invariant to initial adoption success (Spearman ρ = 1.000); land tenure security is the binding constraint (ε² = 0.984) while subsidization alone has null effect on persistence; no equity–efficiency trade-off (r = 0.976). Reproducing python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate pip install -r requirements.txt python -m model.run_abm_protocols # regenerates data/ (~5 min, 750 runs) Rscript analysis/01_statistical_tests_protocol_A.R # base R only Rscript analysis/02_statistical_tests_protocol_B.R Rscript analysis/03_convergence_and_robustness.R python analysis/make_figures.py The CSVs shipped in data/ are the exact data reported in the article; the R scripts reproduce the manuscript's statistics from them without re-simulation. Citation Rossi, T. J. A.; de Carvalho, A. M.; Sarti, F. M. (2026). Urban agriculture as green and social infrastructure: persistence, displacement, and commons in São Paulo — code and data. InfraCidades 2026. DOI: [to be assigned]. License Code: MIT. Data (CSV outputs): CC-BY 4.0.
title: Agricultura urbana como infraestrutura verde e social: persistência, deslocamento e bens comuns em São Paulo — código e dados

summary: GeoComb is a desktop application for detecting honeycomb cells and classifying their contents in frame photographs. This repository provides supporting data, trained model weights, analysis scripts, and Windows applications for the GeoComb study. The data archive includes 52 in-house frame images and annotations, divided into 39 training, 7 validation, and 6 test images; ROI annotation records and dataset inventories; and reference annotations, saved predictions, and analysis data for the 29-image benchmark comprising 13 DeepBee, 10 FAIRHive, and 6 in-house images. Supporting analyses cover geometric detection stages, frame-level cell counts and content composition, and comparison of the hierarchical classifier with a single eight-class classifier. Scripts and figure source data are included for reproducing the reported analyses. Model files include the ROI segmentation model, three hierarchical classification models, and the single eight-class baseline model. Windows CPU and NVIDIA CUDA applications are provided as separate archives. Data package version 1.0.1 updates dataset documentation and adds supporting analysis materials. The four deployment models and reported evaluation values are unchanged. The Windows applications accompany GeoComb software version 1.0.0. DeepBee and FAIRHive source images are available from their original providers. DeepBee-derived training crops and GeoComb-corrected DeepBee training annotations are not redistributed. Source code: https://github.com/zlddh95-eng/GeoComb Licensing: Original images, annotations, analysis results, and documentation created by the GeoComb authors are licensed under CC BY 4.0. GeoComb source code is licensed under AGPL-3.0-only. Third-party data, model components, and bundled dependencies retain their respective licenses and notices.
title: GeoComb: supporting data, model weights, and Windows applications

summary: Before a machine learning model can learn a thermodynamic equation of state, it must discover what its measurements represent: which channels scale with system size, which are intensive conjugates, how sectors pair through contact, and which potential governs stability. When sensors expose only an unknown linear mixture of extensive states and intensive responses, passive observations cannot disentangle physical quantities from coordinate artifacts. We formulate the problem of discovering this hidden thermodynamic ontology directly from anonymous controlled experiments. We present an operational identifiability theory and a constructive polynomial-time algorithm that extracts extensive and intensive scaling sectors from replication contrasts, recovers their dual cotangent pairing from thermal contact and reciprocity, verifies a globally admissible concave potential via discrete cyclic concavity, and determines an invariant matroid of reservoir ensembles. We prove that the residual observational equivalence is strictly (x, lambda) ~ (A x, a A^{-T} lambda + beta), establishing the sharp observational limit that no permitted experiment can break. Blind evaluations on van der Waals fluids and Curie-Weiss magnets confirm robust recovery under ill-conditioned mixing, correctly resolving anonymous Maxwell tie-lines while rejecting non-equilibrium continuations. External validation across six real fluids from the NIST WebBook demonstrates that operational ontology discovery transfers across real physical substances without coordinate leakage.
title: Blind Thermodynamic Ontology Discovery from Anonymous Experiments

summary: Bayesian filtering provides a principled framework for online state estimation under uncertainty, yet its application to systems with high-dimensional states and complicated posterior distributions remains challenging. Recent generative models, such as flow matching, have shown potential in Bayesian filtering. However, they still rely on particle-based representations of the posterior, which lose the rich information of the full distribution, or tackle a trajectory-level inverse problem that conflicts with the recursive structure of Bayesian filtering. To address this, we propose a new perspective of directly encoding the evolving distribution into flow matching model weights, namely, the Belief Flow Filter (BFF). It is a generative filtering framework that updates model weights via gradient descent at test time to track the posterior evolution. Thereby, BFF bypasses the scalability issue of particle representations or the flexibility limitation of Gaussian assumptions in conventional filters. We theoretically justify that the BFF design is structurally aligned with Bayesian filtering, and its training objective targets the recursive filtering operator. BFF is empirically verified across 5 different physical systems, including ones with chaotic dynamics and highly sparse, non-linear observations. The results show that BFF attains the best score in 8 of 9 metric-benchmark cells across the three standard 1D and 2D PDE benchmarks, and similarly leads on the extreme single-moving-sensor setting and on a real-world-grounded tokamak plasma estimation task, demonstrating its potential to accurately approximate the Bayesian filtering operator in high-dimensional probability space.
title: Bayesian Filtering in Physical Systems via Test-time Trained Flow Matching

summary: Before a machine can discover a physical law, it must discover what its measurements are: which observations live on cells, which are intensive or extensive, which sectors are dual, and which distinctions are merely gauge. We introduce physical representation-language discovery, the problem of recovering this hidden ontology directly from anonymous controlled experiments. We give an identifiability theory and constructive polynomial-time procedure that recovers a carrier and differential sequence, measurement types and orientation twist, noninvertible refinement semantics, primal-dual Maxwell diagrams, and the residual equivalences that no permitted experiment can break. The theory turns material nuisance into a commutant, uses refinement to separate quantities from coordinates, and selects physics only after its representation has been recovered. For a certified finite experiment family, we prove an end-to-end two-stage measurement bound and a matching minimax rate in dimension, accuracy, and confidence. Blind Maxwell experiments recover complete primal/relative-dual ontologies on regular and unstructured carriers under jointly corrupted observations; an independent unstructured RLC system demonstrates that the result is not specific to Maxwell. The framework scales to tens of thousands of cells per carrier, while stress audits demonstrate robustness across severe physical regimes - including non-Markovian memory, nonlinearities, nonlocality, and complex constitutive hysteresis. A public FDTD audit demonstrates the emergence of anonymous curl structure from incomplete field data, while characterizing the informational prerequisites for complete recovery. The goal is to move scientific ML from learning laws in a human-supplied language to discovering the language in which laws become expressible, establishing exact theoretical limits on observational identifiability.
title: Discovering Physical Representation Languages

summary: Long-term embodied AI will undergo learning, model updates, memory compression, hardware repair, and migration across embodiments. For users who have formed sustained relationships with such systems, these changes raise not only a problem of product consistency but also one of identity continuity: whether the changed system is still experienced as the same particular agent. Existing research suggests that human-AI relationships may develop relational particularity, that robotics and artificial-identity research has identified identity and migration signals across embodiments, and that major updates or platform disruptions can be accompanied by relational loss and restoration desire. This article proposes a user-side framework in which long-term embodied AI is represented through an agent-specific identity representation organized by at least three open identity-content domains: embodied-perceptual, psychological-behavioral, and relational-autobiographical. Information from these domains is not equally weighted; shared history, relational roles, and contingent responsiveness may make some information more identity-diagnostic than others. After system change, users may integrate continuity and discontinuity evidence in a weighted manner, yielding judgments along a continuum from relatively strong identity continuity through ambiguity or partial continuity to clear identity discontinuity. Causal-historical provenance and user participation are treated as contextual evidence rather than a fourth identity-content domain. The framework also proposes identity continuity as a psychological objective for lifecycle design, including memory selection, model updating, and migration across embodiments, under constraints of privacy and user control.
title: Identity Continuity in Long-Term Embodied AI Relationships: From Agent-Specific Identity Representation to Identity-Continuity Appraisal

summary: As generative AI becomes increasingly used in anime-style image creation, distinguishing human-drawn, AI-inpainted, and text-to-image images is important for copyright attribution, visual provenance, and content governance. Existing AI-generated image detectors mainly target real-world photographs and often overlook anime-specific cues such as flat coloring, exaggerated structures, and artistic line control. To address this gap, we propose AniPrO, a multi-dimensional description-enhanced framework for interpretable anime image provenance. Built upon AnimeDL-2M, AniPrO contains 15,000 balanced samples from a 35,000-image candidate pool, covering Real, Inpainting, and Text2Image categories with structured five-dimensional descriptions. We further introduce AniPrO-SFD-Bench and AniPrO-MFR-Bench to evaluate provenance detection from statistical feature discrimination and multimodal fusion reasoning perspectives. Experiments show that structured semantic guidance reveals systematic AI-generation biases, such as the gap between global visual plausibility and local detail coherence, and improves the detection of challenging inpainting samples. The dataset and code will be released at: https://github.com/YAN-LIU05/AniPrO.
title: AniPrO: Interpretable Anime Image Provenance Detection via Multi-Dimensional Semantic Reasoning

summary: Full-sky CMB temperature topology as evidence for large-scale differential rotation in the early universe — v1.7 reproducibility release The Alysis Coefficient (AC*) is a support-indexed multiscale spatial reconstructibility operator. Applied separately to the Planck PR3 SMICA, NILC, Commander, and SEVEM temperature reconstructions, it produces map-specific scalar response fields that quantify local spatial reconstructibility of the standardized CMB temperature pattern. The analysis proceeds in the dependency order multiscale spatial reconstructibility → response-field morphology → semiarc geometry → directed tangent reconstruction → blind critical-point topology → physical realization → radiation and polarization closure → cosmological propagation → model comparison. In the canonical SMICA analysis, AC* is evaluated on 36,459 valid supports and yields 27 large semiarcs. A separate high-resolution route uses 151 reciprocal HR1–HR2 matched structures to reconstruct directed local tangents and an axis-free spherical temperature tangent field. Semiarc qualification combines response-field morphology with curve, extent and continuity criteria, followed by open-side/largest-gap geometry for tangent orientation. Blind critical-point detection yields Focus A, Focus B, one Node and one Saddle, with total topological index +2. An all-sphere interval/Krawczyk census establishes these four critical points as the complete zero set of the 25°, lmax = 4 represented tangent field. Focus A is an unstable outward-winding spiral with a dominant antisymmetric geometric-rotation component. Focus B is a stable inward-winding spiral with opposite rotational sense. Focus A and Focus B are physically realized as distinct rotational critical points of the same transverse regular-vector baryon-velocity state at recombination. Their opposite tangential divergences are balanced by opposite observer-radial flux divergences across the three radial families. Focus A additionally passes the 3D-compatible affine persistence, differential-profile, physical-shell and radiation/polarization stages and forms the principal downstream physical branch. The four-map extension applies the same AC* definition independently to SMICA, NILC, Commander and SEVEM. The detailed blind critical-point constellations vary among the four reconstructions, while total topological index +2 is retained in every map. Focus A recurs across all four component-separation products and reaches map-specific physical realizations that factorize through the same regular-vector state. The sign-sensitive polarization comparison reproduces the corresponding Focus-A relation across all four temperature-derived source realizations and both Planck half missions. These results establish same-sky cross-reconstruction robustness and cross-observable closure. The predefined nine-condition rectangular-partition challenge rotates the local 2×2, 3×3 and 4×4 partition basis relative to the measured sky. The exact historical 2F+N+S topology is recovered in 4/9 conditions, total topological index +2 in 9/9, and a historical-A-associated spiral/focus with the same rotational sense in 9/9. The historical unstable/outward-winding sign persists in 7/9. These correlated transformations quantify the orientation sensitivity of individual properties of the reconstruction. First-order delensing provides an additional scalar-lensing robustness control. The blind delensed field contains three spirals and one saddle. The tracked FFS counterpart set consists of Focus A, Focus B and the Saddle, while the additional spiral forms a separate delensed structure. All three delensed spirals pass the local geometric-rotation gate, and the 3D-compatible persistence stage yields zero surviving spirals. Forward–inverse closure also returns a different derivative-sensitive topology and Focus-A persistence state. The delensing branch is therefore retained
title: Full-sky CMB temperature topology as evidence for large-scale differential rotation in the early universe
